primary_meaning: In most Christian teaching, midnight symbolizes the darkest hour—a time of crisis, judgment, and sudden divine intervention—and, above all in the New Testament, the unexpected moment of the Lord's coming, calling believers to watchfulness. Preachers commonly present midnight as the point of deepest darkness at which God decisively acts, whether in judgment (the death of Egypt's firstborn) or in deliverance and visitation (the bridegroom's arrival in the parable of the ten virgins).
primary_basis: Exodus 12:29 (at midnight the LORD struck down the firstborn of Egypt)
Matthew 25:6 (at midnight the cry went out, 'Behold, the bridegroom comes')
Mark 13:35 (watch, for you do not know when the master comes—evening, midnight, cockcrow, or morning)
Exodus 11:4 (about midnight I will go out into the midst of Egypt)
Acts 16:25-26 (at midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang, and God delivered them)

alternatives.meaning: Midnight as the hour of eschatological watchfulness specifically—the unknown time of Christ's return and the parousia, urging readiness (an emphasis narrower than general divine intervention)
Midnight as the hour of prayer, worship, and devotion—praising God in the depths of trial, often linked to deliverance following faithful prayer
basis: Psalm 119:62 (at midnight I rise to give thanks)
Job 35:10 (songs in the night, often paired homiletically)

alternatives.meaning: Midnight as sudden judgment and death striking without warning—God's visitation upon the wicked
basis: Job 34:20 (in a moment they die, at midnight the people are shaken)
Luke 12:20 ('this night your soul is required of you,' often connected homiletically)

alternatives.meaning: Midnight as spiritual darkness, despair, or the 'dark night of the soul'—a devotional/mystical reading of personal crisis before dawn's deliverance, popular in preaching (e.g., 'a knock at midnight' traditions)
basis: Luke 11:5-8 (the friend who comes at midnight asking for bread)
Psalm 30:5 (weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning—used supportively)

alternatives.meaning: Midnight as importunity/persistence in prayer—the inconvenient hour highlighting bold asking
Midnight as a merely literal time marker with no fixed symbolic value, its significance varying entirely by context (the position of many critical commentators)

notes: Midnight is a recurring biblical motif rather than a term with a single fixed symbolic definition. There is broad, recognizable agreement that it connotes the darkest hour and sudden divine action—judgment in Exodus, the bridegroom's arrival in Matthew 25, deliverance in Acts 16—but the emphasis (judgment, watchfulness, prayer, despair-before-dawn) varies by tradition and passage. Homiletical traditions (e.g., African-American preaching, Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'A Knock at Midnight') have strengthened the 'crisis/dark night before deliverance' reading. Because these strands overlap without one universally codified definition, consensus should be described as a cluster of related meanings centered on darkness, crisis, and divine visitation, not a single settled interpretation.
